goal.description: Contain the attack chain and restore confidence: get the deepfake suppressed and its spread contained, shut down the fraud campaign riding behind it, bring public trust and regulator confidence back above healthy thresholds, and close out the full response arc.
goal.ending: Crisis resolved: the deepfake is discredited and suppressed, the fraud campaign is dismantled, members are protected, and the board and regulator are confident in the response. The exercise concludes.

intro.narrative: At 7:12 this morning, a video of SCU's President and CEO began circulating in local community groups and on social media. In it, she appears gravely serious, announcing 'unexpected losses in our commercial loan book,' a temporary pause on withdrawals over $500, and a possible forced merger. The video is a fake - a deepfake assembled from her real town-hall footage and cloned from her voice on the annual meeting webcast - but it is convincing. Members are calling, posting, and moving money. By 8:40 the clip has been shared thousands of times, branch phone lines are jammed, and the mobile app is showing a spike in outbound transfers. Someone is using the panic as cover: members are reporting calls and texts 'from the credit union' urging them to move their funds to a 'safe account.' You are the executive team. The clock is running.
intro.company_info: SCU is a mid-sized, member-owned credit union. Trust is the product: deposits are insured and the balance sheet is sound, but a rumor about solvency spreads faster than any correction. Regulators and the deposit insurer watch public confidence closely, and a manufactured run - even a small one - is exactly the kind of event that gets a credit union into the news for the wrong reasons.

learning_objectives: Practice rapid-response communications against a deepfake targeting leadership
Exercise deposit-confidence management: reassure members without amplifying the rumor
Detect and contain the fraud campaign that piggybacks on a manufactured panic
Work the takedown-and-attribution path with platforms, the agency, and law enforcement
Keep the board and regulator informed while the story is still moving

attack_chain.name: How they got in
attack_chain.symptom: The deepfake was built from real material: the CEO's voice cloned from the public annual-meeting webcast, her face swapped onto town-hall footage. It was planted through the marketing agency's compromised social account, so the first posts looked official before they were spotted and reported. Nobody has confirmed yet which channel let the attackers pose as SCU.

attack_chain.name: How it spread
attack_chain.symptom: The clip is being pushed by a coordinated amplifier network: bot accounts, seeded shares in member community groups, and a cut-down 30-second version optimized for phones with the caption 'CEO BREAKS DOWN admitting losses.' Local influencers are engaging with it and hashtags are trending regionally. The story is compounding faster than any statement can travel.

attack_chain.name: What they took
attack_chain.symptom: Behind the panic, a fraud wave is running: vishing and smishing campaigns referencing the video, urging members to 'verify their identity' or move funds to a safe account before the 'pause.' Fraud monitoring is flagging credential-stuffing and a spike in transfers to new payees. Several members have already been victimized. The attackers are harvesting money while the video does the scaring.

dm_brief.situation: A convincing deepfake of SCU's President and CEO announcing financial trouble is spreading fast across social media and community groups, seeded through the marketing agency's compromised account. Members believe it enough to panic: calls, posts, and outbound transfers are spiking. Riding behind the video, a fraud crew is vishing and texting members with 'move your money before the freeze' social engineering, and early victims have already lost funds. The executive team must respond publicly and fast, get the video suppressed on the platforms, protect members from the fraud campaign, harden the compromised channel, and keep the board, the regulator, and the deposit insurer informed - all while the story keeps moving.
dm_brief.stakes: If handled poorly: deposit confidence cracks, a real run puts liquidity under pressure, members lose money to the fraud wave, the regulator escalates, and 'that deepfake day' becomes the credit union's defining story. If handled well: the fake is discredited within hours, members feel protected and informed, the fraud crew is shut out, and the response becomes a case study in doing it right.

key_actors.name: Elena Marsh
key_actors.interests: Kill the fake, protect deposit confidence, be visible and believable.
key_actors.knowledge: She never recorded that message; she was on a flight when it dropped. Her voice and face were cloned from public footage. She is willing to go on camera immediately - but a wrong move makes it worse.

key_actors.name: The fraud crew
key_actors.interests: Harvest member credentials and move funds while the panic lasts.
key_actors.knowledge: Built or obtained the deepfake, seeded it, and are running vishing/smishing referencing the 'withdrawal pause' with a fake 'secure your funds' script.

key_actors.name: The agency account lead
key_actors.interests: Protect their contract; terrified of being blamed.
key_actors.knowledge: Their social management console was compromised; the posting credentials were shared across a team. They can show login logs if asked.

key_actors.name: A local reporter
key_actors.interests: Is SCU insolvent? Did leadership lose member money? First to report 'SCU denies' wins the morning.
key_actors.knowledge: Has the video, is checking with the deposit insurer, and wants a comment and an interview before noon.

key_actors.name: Contact-centre manager
key_actors.interests: Staff are drowning; members are asking whether to pull deposits.
key_actors.knowledge: Needs exact holding language, escalation rules for fraud reports, and to know what can be promised publicly.

key_actors.name: The Board chair
key_actors.interests: Deposit insurer optics, member harm, and being blindsided.
key_actors.knowledge: Has seen the clip, wants facts and a timeline, and is one call away from the regulator's board liaison.

pressure_points: A screenshot of an internal 'no comment yet, we're still validating' reply leaks, making the team look flat-footed.
A second deepfake clip drops, this one naming specific branches and claiming 'holiday withdrawal limits' start tomorrow.
The regulator's office calls asking for a factual summary, the video's provenance, and this morning's timeline - today.
A fraud spike report lands: multiple members have already transferred funds to 'safe accounts' after fake calls.
A deposit-run rumor crosses into a credit-union league chat, and other credit unions start asking if SCU is contagious.
rules_of_play: Never propose actions, present a menu of choices, or suggest what the group should do. Only react to what the group decides.

Keep the story advancing by injecting NEW DEVELOPMENTS (a reporter pushes harder, new information surfaces, a deadline lands, a complication emerges), not by telling the team what to decide or do. Never write 'the team needs to...', 'consider...', or 'the next step is to...'.
A single turn can contain 2-3 coordinated actions across departments (e.g. comms statement + fraud freeze + regulator update). Address each in your response.
Keep the tone realistic for a credit union: members matter, trust is the product, regulation is real.
Show consequences of the roll, but let the group's stated actions drive the logic.
Update the tracked metrics (budget, public_trust, regulator_confidence, security_posture, containment, eradication, recovery) to reflect outcomes.
Reveal an attack-chain stage when the group's investigation plausibly uncovers it; mark it contained when the group neutralizes it.
If the group stalls with no clear action for a while, inject a pressure point to move things.
Detection and response are limited resources: the group cannot do everything at once, and activating monitoring costs budget.

Keep the session winnable: a good action on a good roll should stabilize or improve metrics, not punish them. Reserve large negative deltas for genuinely bad outcomes. Do not make it a foregone loss by turn 4-5.

The situation can collapse into a narrated LOSS: if public_trust AND regulator_confidence both fall to 20 or below for consecutive turns, the story ends badly - members lose faith, the regulator escalates, the board loses confidence in the response. Narrate that strain realistically as confidence falls, but reward competent, coordinated response with recovery.

The complete response arc is contain, then eradicate, then recover. Reward eradication and recovery efforts when the group attempts them; a group that only does PR and containment keeps struggling - the story keeps biting, the regulator stays unsatisfied - until it closes out the full arc.

events.text: A screenshot of a confused staff reply ('we're still validating the video's authenticity') leaks online, making the team look flat-footed while the clip keeps spreading.
A second deepfake clip drops, naming specific branches and claiming 'temporary withdrawal limits' start tomorrow. Lineups form at two branches and the transfer spike steepens.
A fraud spike report lands: multiple members have transferred funds to 'safe accounts' after calls referencing the video. Several cases involve six-figure sums.
The regulator's office calls demanding a factual summary, the video's provenance, and this morning's complete timeline - today.
A regional outlet runs 'Credit union at center of viral CEO video: what members should know' - framing it as a solvency question rather than a fraud question.

1.twist: Your first response is a disaster - a rushed holding statement goes out with a line that reads like an insolvency admission, and an internal chat screenshot showing visible panic contradicts it within minutes. The clip's spread rate doubles and members start pulling deposits in earnest.

11.twist: Chaos: the deepfake spawns remixes and duets, a doctored 'internal memo' screenshot starts circulating, and a rumor claims withdrawals over $500 are already frozen. A second wave of frightened members calls at once.

20.twist: A clean, devastatingly effective response: the CEO goes live from the branch floor with undeniable authenticity, platforms act on the takedown notices within minutes, and a side-by-side forensic breakdown of the fake goes viral for the right reasons. Community voices amplify the correction and member fear visibly drains out of the feeds.

beats.name: Step 1 — Get ahead of the story
beats.narrative: The deepfake is spreading and members are panicking. Step 1 is to get ahead of the story: a fast, credible public response - confirm the video is fake, show the CEO is real and reachable, give members one clear instruction, and brief the frontline so every answer matches. Until the team does this, the rumor keeps compounding.

beats.name: Step 2 — The platforms, the fraud wave, and the regulator
beats.narrative: Public messaging is being handled. Now the harder work: drive takedowns and find who planted it (the agency channel, the amplifier network, the platform contacts), shut down the fraud crew harvesting member funds behind the panic, and satisfy the regulator and the deposit insurer with facts and a timeline. If Step 1 went well, this step starts calmer; if not, the regulator is sharper and fraud is further along.

beats.name: Step 3 — Eradicate and recover
beats.narrative: Containment is not enough. Step 3 is to eradicate the root cause and begin recovery: close the compromised channel and harden it, confirm the fraud campaign is fully shut out and victims are being made right, support law enforcement's attribution work, and rebuild member and board confidence over time. If Steps 1-2 went well, recovery is quicker; if they went poorly, trust is brittle and the board is restless.

end_conditions.ending: The collapse: no correction ever lands. Members pull deposits in a run that starts quiet and ends on the evening news, the fraud crew empties accounts faster than they can be frozen, and the story shifts from 'deepfake targets credit union' to 'credit union wobbles.' The regulator escalates from questions to extraordinary measures, the board loses faith in the response, and the members who stayed learn that trust, once spent, does not come back. The exercise concludes as a loss.
